A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same QR-based attention-flow steganography work, renamed from PPRSteg to RMSteg. Their supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends with references despite mentioning supplementary material; v2 includes Appendices A-C. Later disclosures can be distinguished from explicitly documented method changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original steganography experiments, printing-and-photography tests, security evaluations and component ablations in Tables 1-3.

after.justification: v2 reports original comparative experiments, shooting-condition and payload tests, ablations, and appendix tampering and screen-photography results.

M1.justification: v2 adds learnable invertible token fusion before AttnFlow and a simulated QR-scanning constraint on the transition network. Its training objective also replaces v1's PatchGAN adversarial losses with LPIPS supervision and the transition loss (v1 Section 3.4; v2 Sections 3.3-3.6). These change the procedure beyond renaming.

E1.justification: COCO and generated QR-code data remain central. v2 removes the IStego100K-based steganalysis evaluation and adds evaluation under mixed distortions, image tampering and screen photography, substantially changing task and environmental coverage.

E2.justification: The principal comparisons replace RIIS and RIIS† with StegaStamp and StegaStamp†, while retaining ISN† and HiNet†. v1 reports reproducing RIIS; v2 explicitly declines that comparison because its code and pretrained model are unavailable.

E3.justification: Reported image resolution changes from 144×144 to 224×224, training from 45K to 50K iterations, and batching from 64 to eight per GPU. Table 1 changes noise/JPEG settings, and ablation evaluation switches to mixed distortions. v2 also introduces controlled shooting conditions, QR versions 5-8 and tampering-rate protocols, while removing security metrics.

E4.justification: v2 adds ITF ablation and CNN replacement controls, distortion-severity sweeps, shooting-condition and capacity analyses, and tampering and screen-photography tests. Appendices also investigate QR-decoding errors and homogeneous-image failures. The earlier QR-transition, cross-attention and block-count ablations remain in revised form.

E5.justification: v1 Tables 1 and 3 state error intervals of ±0.003 for TRA and ±0.005 for EMR; v2 omits these without replacement uncertainty estimates. Neither version specifies training-seed counts. Selecting the best of five photographs remains, so this is not evidence of increased repetitions.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the proposed method's PSNR/LPIPS values of 23.826/0.1852 with 32.883/0.0707 under revised methods and resolution, preventing a same-setting performance comparison. v2 adds shooting, capacity, tampering and expanded ablation results, removes security results, and reports that omitting QR transition slightly improves decoding under its new ablation setting.

T1.justification: v2 adds the mathematical definition and inverse of token fusion, T′=MT and T=M⁻¹T′, and formalizes the scanning-error transition loss in Equation S1. The underlying normalizing-flow coupling equations remain essentially unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: v2 reframes the contribution around robust, high-capacity message embedding and makes ITF an explicit principal contribution. It drops v1's explicit security-superiority claim and changes the QR-transition contribution from improving decoding accuracy to maintaining it while improving image quality.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the interpretation that QR transition improves both quality and decoding with an information-loss tradeoff. It adds explanations involving token mixing, artifact distribution and redundancy under tampering, discusses mismatches between module error and recognizability, and identifies failures on homogeneous images and limits on large payloads (Appendices B-C).

D1.justification: Appendices A-B supply previously unavailable tokenizer/detokenizer specifications, QR-scanning kernel and threshold details, distortion parameters, metric implementation and training time. They also document the printer, phone, print dimensions, shooting geometry and cropping workflow. These substantially improve reproducibility; newly disclosed details alone do not establish implementation changes.

R1.justification: Most related-work coverage remains. v2 adds supporting references such as ArtCoder, Art-up and matrix inversion, explicitly distinguishes ITF's token mixing from GLOW's channel mixing, and removes references associated with the discarded security evaluation. The positioning increasingly emphasizes capacity alongside quality and robustness.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and substantial method and experimental passages are rewritten around RMSteg and message embedding. Method exposition gains a separate overview, training details move into organized appendices, and the experimental narrative replaces the security section with capacity analysis. This exceeds a terminology-only revision.

P2.justification: v2 switches to a two-column layout, adds an introductory demonstration, redraws the pipeline for ITF, and reworks comparison and ablation displays. New distortion curves, shooting/capacity tables, explanatory diagrams and appendix galleries substantially expand the visual presentation; the security table disappears.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves substantial reproducibility gaps through Appendices A-B and strengthens architectural and robustness evidence with targeted ablations, controlled shooting tests, tampering analysis and explicit failure cases. These gains outweigh the loss of RIIS/security comparisons and the earlier, unexplained error intervals, although those removals reduce evidential breadth and uncertainty reporting. The improvement rests on stronger documentation and analysis, not on treating changed-setting scores as controlled performance gains.
